apply.label: Reverse the two events
apply.prompt: Something has just landed. Reverse it?

riders.note: The **defender's** event, not the attacker's. The trigger is "You or an ally within 30 feet takes damage", so it is `damage-received` — `damage-applied` is "damage from this actor's item landed on a target", which is the opposite creature. Driven live on `damage-applied` the reaction was never offered at all. Landing on the attacker is what sends the 2d6 to the triggering creature; the nested `self` sends the resistance back to whoever was hit.

apply.label: Reverse the two events
apply.prompt: An ally within 30 feet has been hurt. Reverse it?

riders.note: S-63b's other half: *“You **or an ally within 30 feet** takes damage from a creature you can see.”* `damage-received` is the defender's own event, so when the ally is hit the engine reads the **ally's** items and the Quincy's Technique is not among them — which is why this clause was recorded ❌ twice before the `ally-damaged` event existed. Identical to the rider above in every other respect: `trigger: true` still sends the 2d6 to the creature that struck, and the resistance still lands on whoever was hurt. The one difference from the rider above is where the resistance goes: on `damage-received` the Quincy **is** the target of the trigger, so it lands on them by default; here the target of the trigger is the ally, and `trigger: "ally"` is the address for that.

description.value:
Trigger You or an ally within 30 feet takes damage from a creature you can see.

You reverse the two events. The triggering creature takes @Damage[2d6[spirit]] damage, and the target of the trigger gains resistance equal to your level against the triggering damage.

Heightened (+2) The damage increases by 1d6.

Refined (9th) You additionally gain Licht Regen.

This is Bakudō #81 with the damage reflected instead of absorbed, which is exactly what Antithesis does in canon.
